passage:
Placement cell note, Thursday. Vishal came for a mock interview. On the panel's questions Vishal answered in clear, polished English, calm and confident. Good. Afterwards I walked out to the car park and saw Vishal speaking to the college driver, Bhola Ram. The tone changed at once: Hindi in the driver's local dialect, quick and easy, a laugh, a hand on the shoulder.
Then a second scene: when two juniors approached, Vishal answered them in fast English and turned away, and the juniors' faces fell. I asked Vishal to talk with me afterwards. We talked about how language can bring people in or keep them out. Vishal said, "I didn't notice." Next day I saw Vishal greet the juniors in Hindi first.
Trisha, placement officer

qa.q: Who was the college driver that Vishal spoke to in the car park?
qa.a: The college driver was Bhola Ram.

qa.q: What might Vishal have been feeling when saying "I didn't notice"?
qa.a: Vishal was probably surprised and a little embarrassed. The words suggest the switch had happened without thought, and Vishal had not meant to leave the juniors out.

qa.q: What did Trisha do after seeing the switch, and what changed the next day?
qa.a: Trisha talked with Vishal about how language can include or exclude. The next day Vishal greeted the juniors in Hindi first.

qa.q: How might the juniors have felt when Vishal answered them in fast English and turned away?
qa.a: The juniors probably felt dismissed or small, since their faces fell. A friendly switch to Hindi the next day would tell them they were welcome.

grounding: A young adult moves into polished English for an interview and into a local tongue with the driver, and learns that language can include or exclude.

passage:
Saturday night. Interview went okay, I think. I spoke English the whole time, and used long words, and I felt very grown-up.
But something bothered me. This morning, before my cousins arrived, I chatted to Lakshmi akka in Tamil in the kitchen, and we laughed about the burnt dosa. Then my cousins came in, and I heard myself say to her in English, "Could you please bring the tea?" in that stiff voice, and Lakshmi akka looked at me strangely and said nothing.
I don't know why I did it. I think I wanted my cousins to see me as someone who employs people, not someone who jokes with them. That is an awful reason.
I'll say sorry tomorrow, in Tamil.
— Vandana

qa.q: What did Vandana say to Lakshmi akka in English when the cousins came in?
qa.a: Vandana said, "Could you please bring the tea?" in a stiff voice.

qa.q: How did Vandana feel after looking back on the morning?
qa.a: Vandana felt uneasy and ashamed. Calling the English request "an awful reason" shows a guilty conscience about signalling status.

qa.q: What did Vandana decide to do about it, and why is that a good step?
qa.a: Vandana plans to say sorry the next day in Tamil, the language they share warmly. That repairs the hurt and shows respect.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi akka have felt when the tone changed to stiff English?
qa.a: Lakshmi akka may have felt hurt or shut out, since the warm chatting turned into a formal order. Looking strangely and saying nothing suggests the change was felt.

grounding: A young adult uses polished English at an interview and local tongue at home, and notices using language to signal status with someone hurts.
